To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the response of a simple model neuron depends on the synaptic time constant in a nontrivial way and that this neuron becomes a good coincidence detector when the time constants of the synapses are very different from each other.

the firing rate of a simple model neuron depends on the synaptic time constants in the following way: the neuron is most sensitive to the fastest time scale and less sensitive to the slowest time scale.

the response of a simple integrate-and-fire neuron is a function of the synaptic time constants and that this neuron is a coincidence detector when the synaptic time constant is larger than the membrane time constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of synaptic filtering on neuronal firing.
the study of the effect of synaptic filtering on simple model neurons, and the role of the synaptic time scales on the firing properties of these neurons.
understanding the role of synaptic filtering in neuronal computation, and the implications that this has for the design of spiking neuron-based artificial networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in a neuron with synaptic time constants longer than the membrane time constant, the firing rate is proportional to the number of spikes arriving in a short time window, and is not affected by the precise timing of the input spikes.
the neuron responds best to the fast component of the input current, and that the neuron is a coincidence detector only when the fast synaptic component is absent.
, for a given input, the neuron will respond to the most relevant features of the input, and the response will be determined by a competition among the different synaptic filters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the neuron is able to detect the occurrence of a spike train with a time constant much shorter (by a factor of two) than the synaptic time constant, but is unable to detect the time of occurrence of the spikes.
the neuron responds best to the input with the synaptic timescale closest to the membrane time constant.
the response of the neuron is a weighted sum of the input currents, where the weights are determined by the synaptic filters and the membrane time constant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neuron's response depends on the relative values of the different synaptic time constants.
the neuron response is determined by the time scale of the slowest input, and not by the fastest one, as it is usually believed.
the response of the neuron to its inputs depends on the time scales of the synaptic filters.
